title: Empatica Embrace seizure alert reaches Morgan McGrath's mother, who calls paramedics after a seizure left the 26-year-old teacher not breathing (Fulton, Missouri)
summary: IEEE Spectrum (6 Feb 2018): an Embrace wristband alerted the mother of Morgan McGrath, 26, of Fulton, Mo., during a seizure about 15 months earlier; she called paramedics and McGrath survived.
account: Elie Dolgin reported in IEEE Spectrum on 6 February 2018 (the publication date is used because the article dates the seizure only to 'fifteen months ago', about November 2016) that Morgan McGrath, a 26-year-old teacher from Fulton, Missouri, 'suffered an epileptic seizure that left her unresponsive, frothing at the mouth, with blue lips, and not breathing'; her wrist-worn Embrace device sent her mother an alert, her mother called the paramedics, and 'thanks to a timely response, McGrath is alive and well today'. The article explains that the device records skin conductance and three-axis accelerometer data and 'uses a proprietary algorithm to signal when someone is having a convulsive seizure', with the app sending a text or call to pre-specified caregivers, and that in testing on 135 patients over more than 6,500 hours it 'correctly identified nearly every single seizure'. The FDA cleared Embrace (Empatica S.r.l.) under 510(k) K172935 on 26 January 2018, after the McGrath event; the 510(k) summary describes an on-board algorithm validated against video-EEG that, when a likely generalised tonic-clonic seizure is detected, messages the Alert app to call and text designated caregivers. A later prospective multicentre study by Empatica staff with hospital co-authors (Onorati et al. 2021) reports sensitivity of 0.92 in children and 0.94 in adults for a predefined machine-learning algorithm, and an independent Montreal epilepsy-monitoring-unit study (Jahani et al. 2026) found the Embrace2 detected all 16 convulsive seizures that occurred while worn and working, with alerts reaching caregivers in 15 of 16 cases and 29 false alarms. The McGrath rescue rests on this single news item; the Empatica case-study abstract (Regalia, Onorati, Picard, American Epilepsy Society) named by the earlier verifier could not be located, and no second account of the McGrath event was found.
purpose: Built to detect convulsive seizures from electrodermal activity and motion and to summon designated caregivers; the alert to McGrath's mother was that purpose.
system: Empatica Embrace wrist-worn seizure detection (electrodermal activity and accelerometer, on-board algorithm) with the Alert smartphone app
model_version: Embrace (the article does not state the generation); echoes concern Embrace2
segment: Prescription wearable seizure monitor used at home
taxonomy_note: No health type exists; Accessibility chosen, as in the Apple Watch arrhythmia record, because the device made seizure monitoring available at home outside clinical settings. Protective response rather than harm prevented because the only source is one news report whose outcome attribution ('thanks to a timely response') is the journalist's, with no medical record. Supporting evidence on detection performance comes from a vendor-authored multicentre study, the FDA 510(k) summary and an independent 2026 epilepsy-monitoring-unit evaluation.

ratings.reason: A young woman who was not breathing during a seizure had paramedics summoned by her mother on the device's alert and is reported alive and well; a potentially life-saving response documented only in one news report.

ai_role.statement: Per IEEE Spectrum, the Embrace detected the seizure and its app alerted McGrath's mother, who made the emergency call; the device did not call for help itself. The algorithm is described as proprietary by the article, as an on-board algorithm validated against video-EEG by the FDA summary, and as a predefined machine-learning algorithm by Empatica's own 2021 study. The McGrath event is known only from this single news item; the AES case-study abstract cited by the earlier verifier was not found.

evidence.quote: A prospective study was conducted for the FDA clearance of an ACM and EDA-based CS-detection device based on a predefined machine learning algorithm.

evidence.title: Prospective evaluation of a seizure detection wearable device for timely interventions in an epilepsy monitoring unit
evidence.quote: Alerts successfully reached caregivers in 15 of 16 cases, with one failure due to a Wi‐Fi disconnection.

produced_by: A convulsive (generalised tonic-clonic) seizure, the only type the device is cleared to detect
The wristband worn and paired with a phone running the Alert app, with a caregiver designated
A caregiver able to reach the patient or call emergency services on receiving the alert
must_hold: Connectivity between watch, phone and caregiver (one of 16 alerts in Montreal failed on a Wi-Fi disconnection)
Caregivers tolerate false alarms (29 in 373 monitoring days in Montreal, mostly from routine movements)
Focal seizures without convulsions are not detected (none of 510 in Montreal)

echoes.setting: Centre hospitalier de l'Université de Montréal epilepsy monitoring unit, 72 patients, April 2024 to June 2025; alerts routed to nursing staff
echoes.source: Jahani et al. (2026) Epilepsia 67(4):1802-1816, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13075604/ (quote: 'The Embrace2 wrist‐worn device detected all 16 FBTCSs/GTCSs that occurred while the device was functioning and worn, but none of 510 FSs.')

echoes.setting: Multicentre epilepsy-monitoring-unit study, 152 patients (85 children), 66 convulsive seizures; detection performance only, no home alerts
echoes.source: Onorati et al. (2021) Front Neurol 12:724904, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8418082/ (sensitivity 0.92 pediatric, 0.94 adult; false alarm rate 1.26 and 0.57 per 24 h)
